summary: A brushed DC motor is two coupled first-order equations, one electrical and one mechanical, linked by the motor constant. You derive them, find the steady-state speed under load and the two time constants, simulate a step response, and check the simulation against the closed-form steady state.
html:
Two equations

The armature is a resistance R and inductance L in series with the back-EMF kω (lesson 1). The rotor is an inertia J with viscous friction b, driven by the motor torque ki and resisted by the load torque TL​:

Ldtdi​=V−Ri−kω,Jdtdω​=ki−bω−TL​.

The same constant k appears twice, as torque per amp (N·m/A) and as volts per rad/s, as the power balance demands.

Steady state

Set both derivatives to zero. From the second, i=(bω+TL​)/k; put it into the first:

ωss​=k2+RbkV−RTL​​.

With no load and negligible friction, ωss​≈V/k: the motor speeds up until its back-EMF nearly cancels the supply. Each unit of load torque costs R/k2 of speed, which is the slope of the torque-speed line (lesson 4).

Two time scales

Small motors usually have L/R≪JR/k2, so the dynamics separate:

  • Electrical time constant τe​=L/R, typically well under a millisecond: the current settles first.
  • Mechanical time constant τm​=k2+RbJR​: with the current always “caught up”, the speed approaches ωss​ exponentially with this time constant.

The transfer function from voltage to speed is (Ls+R)(Js+b)+k2k​, a second-order system with these two poles (Phase 03).

The live motor lab on the home page runs this same model in 3D.

Worked example

A small 12 V motor has R=1.2 Ω, L=0.6 mH, k=0.02 N·m/A, J=3×10−6 kg·m² and b=2×10−6 N·m·s.

  1. No load: ωss​=0.24/(0.0004+0.0000024)=596.4 rad/s, which is 5695 rpm.
  2. With TL​=0.05 N·m: ωss​=(0.24−0.06)/0.0004024=447.3 rad/s.
  3. τe​=0.6 mH/1.2 Ω=0.5 ms and τm​=3×10−6⋅1.2/0.0004024=8.95 ms.
  4. Starting current: V/R=10 A for an instant, while the steady load current is (bω+TL​)/k=2.54 A.

Code it from scratch

dc_motor.py
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

R, L, k, J, b = 1.2, 0.6e-3, 0.02, 3e-6, 2e-6

def deriv(x, V, TL):
    i, w = x
    return np.array([(V - R * i - k * w) / L, (k * i - b * w - TL) / J])

def simulate(V, TL, T=0.08, dt=5e-6):
    x = np.zeros(2); out = [x.copy()]
    for _ in range(int(round(T / dt))):          # classic RK4
        k1 = deriv(x, V, TL); k2 = deriv(x + dt / 2 * k1, V, TL)
        k3 = deriv(x + dt / 2 * k2, V, TL); k4 = deriv(x + dt * k3, V, TL)
        x = x + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4); out.append(x.copy())
    return np.arange(len(out)) * dt, np.array(out)

def steady_speed(V, TL):
    return (k * V - R * TL) / (k * k + R * b)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for TL in (0.0, 0.05):
        t, x = simulate(12.0, TL)
        print(f"T_L = {TL}: simulated {x[-1, 1]:.2f} rad/s, formula {steady_speed(12.0, TL):.2f} rad/s")
        assert abs(x[-1, 1] - steady_speed(12.0, TL)) < 1e-3 * steady_speed(12.0, TL)
    # inrush current approaches V/R, because there is no back-EMF at standstill
    t, x = simulate(12.0, 0.0, T=0.002)
    assert 0.8 * 10 < x[:, 0].max() < 10
    # mechanical time constant: 63 % of final speed after about tau_m (plus a little electrical lag)
    t, x = simulate(12.0, 0.0)
    tau_m = J * R / (k * k + R * b)
    t63 = t[np.argmax(x[:, 1] >= 0.632 * x[-1, 1])]
    assert abs(t63 - tau_m) < 0.1 * tau_m
    # cross-check against the state-space model with SciPy
    sys = signal.StateSpace([[-R / L, -k / L], [k / J, -b / J]], [[1 / L], [0]], [[0, 1]], [[0]])
    ts = np.linspace(0, 0.08, 2001)
    _, y = signal.step(sys, T=ts)
    _, x = simulate(12.0, 0.0, T=0.08, dt=4e-5)
    assert np.max(np.abs(12 * y - x[:, 1])) < 0.5

Exercises

The motor runs at 447 rad/s under a 0.05 N·m load. The supply drops from 12 V to 10 V. What’s the new speed?

Show the solution

ωss​=(0.02⋅10−1.2⋅0.05)/0.0004024=0.14/0.0004024=347.9 rad/s. Speed is linear in voltage at a fixed load, with slope k/(k2+Rb)=49.7 rad/s per volt.

Why can’t you treat this motor as first order if you want to design a 2 kHz current loop?

Show the solution

A 2 kHz loop is fast compared with τe​=0.5 ms (318 Hz). The inductance is exactly what the current loop controls, so the electrical pole must be in the model. The mechanical motion barely changes in that time, so it can be treated as a slowly varying back-EMF disturbance instead (lesson 7).
